title: supplyAsync — fetch user profile
description: Simulate an async user profile fetch using supplyAsync. The task sleeps 500ms to simulate network latency, then returns a user name string.
hints: Use join() to block for result

solution.explanation: CompletableFuture.supplyAsync() runs the Supplier in the ForkJoinPool.commonPool() (or a custom Executor passed as second arg). The main thread continues executing while the async task runs in a pool thread — this is the core benefit. join() blocks until completion and rethrows exceptions unchecked. get() does the same but declares checked exceptions. The print statement before join() often appears before the 'Fetching user...' line, proving true asynchrony.

methodSignatures.description: Runs the Supplier asynchronously in the ForkJoinPool and returns a CompletableFuture<U>.
Same as above but uses the provided Executor instead of ForkJoinPool.
Waits for completion and returns result. Throws unchecked CompletionException on failure.

title: thenApply — transform the result
description: After fetching a product price (as a double), apply a 10% discount using thenApply.

solution.explanation: thenApply() is the CompletableFuture equivalent of map() on a stream. It transforms the result when it arrives, using a Function<T,U>. The transformation runs in the same thread that completed the previous stage (or the calling thread if already complete). No new async task is launched — it's just a synchronous transform chained onto the completion. Use thenApplyAsync() to run the transform in a thread pool.

methodSignatures.method: <U> CompletableFuture<U> thenApply(Function<? super T,? extends U> fn)
methodSignatures.description: When this stage completes, applies fn to the result and returns a new CompletableFuture<U>.

methodSignatures.method: <U> CompletableFuture<U> thenApplyAsync(Function<? super T,? extends U> fn)
methodSignatures.description: Same as thenApply but runs fn asynchronously in ForkJoinPool.

title: thenAccept — consume the result
description: Fetch a notification message async, then consume it with thenAccept to simulate sending an email (print it).
hints: join() the Void future to wait for completion

solution.explanation: thenAccept() applies a Consumer to the result — it consumes the value but produces no new value, returning CompletableFuture<Void>. It's the terminal operation of a CompletableFuture pipeline (like forEach in streams). The void future still needs to be joined/awaited if you want to ensure completion before the program exits. Use thenRun() (no-argument Runnable) when you don't even need the value.

methodSignatures.description: When this stage completes, passes the result to action. Returns CompletableFuture<Void>.
When this stage completes, runs action (no access to result). Returns CompletableFuture<Void>.

title: thenCompose — chain dependent futures
description: Scenario: First fetch a user ID, then use that ID to fetch the user's full profile. These are dependent — you need the user ID before you can fetch the profile.

solution.explanation: thenCompose() is the flatMap of CompletableFuture. It takes a Function that returns a CompletableFuture and flattens it — you get CompletableFuture<String>, not CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<String>>. Use it when step B depends on the result of step A and both are async. Contrast with thenApply (sync transform) and thenCombine (parallel independent tasks). Total time: ~600ms (300+300 sequential).

methodSignatures.method: <U> CompletableFuture<U> thenCompose(Function<? super T, ? extends CompletionStage<U>> fn)
methodSignatures.description: When this stage completes, passes result to fn which returns a new CompletionStage. Returns a flat CompletableFuture<U> (not nested).

title: thenCombine — merge two independent futures
description: Scenario: Fetch a user's name and their loyalty points simultaneously (independent calls). Once both complete, combine them into a greeting string.
hints: thenCombine takes a BiFunction<T, U, R>
Total time should be ~400ms (max of the two), not 700ms

solution.explanation: thenCombine() waits for BOTH futures to complete and combines their results with a BiFunction. Crucially, both futures run in parallel (they were both started immediately), so the total time is approximately max(300, 400) = 400ms — not 700ms. This is the parallel-fan-out pattern for independent async tasks. Compare: thenCompose for sequential dependent tasks, thenCombine for parallel independent tasks.

methodSignatures.method: <U,V> CompletableFuture<V> thenCombine(CompletionStage<? extends U> other, BiFunction<? super T,? super U,? extends V> fn)
methodSignatures.description: When both this stage and other complete, combines their results with fn.

title: allOf — wait for all futures
description: Send 3 notification emails in parallel (each takes ~200ms). Use allOf to wait for all to complete.
hints: To collect results: use thenApply on each future after allOf

solution.explanation: allOf() takes varargs of CompletableFutures and returns a CompletableFuture<Void> that completes when ALL of them complete. It runs all futures in parallel — total time is the slowest individual task, not the sum. Note: allOf returns Void, so to collect actual results you join() each individual future after allOf completes (they are already done at that point, so join() returns immediately).

methodSignatures.description: Returns a CompletableFuture<Void> that completes when ALL given futures complete. If any fail, the result fails.

title: anyOf — first future wins
description: Simulate querying 3 different cache servers simultaneously. Return the result from whichever responds first.
starterCode:
// 3 cache server futures with 400ms, 200ms, 600ms delays
// anyOf returns the first to complete

solution.explanation: anyOf() returns a CompletableFuture<Object> that completes as soon as ANY one of the input futures completes, with that future's result. The other futures continue running (they are not cancelled). The return type is Object — you must cast. Use this for race conditions, hedged requests, or timeout-with-fallback patterns. The slowest futures are simply ignored after the winner completes.

methodSignatures.description: Returns a CompletableFuture<Object> that completes when the FIRST given future completes, with that result.

title: exceptionally — fallback on failure
description: Simulate a payment service that randomly fails. Use exceptionally() to return a default 'PAYMENT_FAILED' response instead of propagating the exception.
starterCode:
// Simulate payment that throws RuntimeException("Payment gateway down")
// Use exceptionally to return "PAYMENT_FAILED" fallback

solution.explanation: exceptionally() is like a catch block for CompletableFuture. It takes a Function<Throwable, T> — if the stage completed exceptionally, the function is applied to produce a fallback value; if the stage completed normally, exceptionally() is a no-op and passes the result through. The Throwable argument is a CompletionException that wraps the original exception — use getCause() for the real cause.

methodSignatures.description: If this stage fails, applies fn to the exception and uses the result as the stage's value. No-op on success.

title: handle — handle both result and exception
description: Use handle() to process both the success and failure cases of an async inventory check. On success format a message; on failure log and return a safe default.
starterCode:
// Async inventory check that may succeed (return 150) or throw
// Use handle() to produce a formatted string in both cases
hints: handle takes a BiFunction<T, Throwable, R>
Exactly one of the two parameters will be null

solution.explanation: handle() is like a finally/catch-and-transform combined. Its BiFunction receives both the result and the exception — exactly one will be null. On success: result is the value, exception is null. On failure: result is null, exception is the CompletionException. Unlike exceptionally() which only fires on failure, handle() always fires. Unlike whenComplete() which consumes the pair and returns the same value, handle() can transform the value (returns CompletableFuture<R>).

methodSignatures.method: <U> CompletableFuture<U> handle(BiFunction<? super T, Throwable, ? extends U> fn)
methodSignatures.description: Always invoked (success or failure). BiFunction receives (result, exception) where one is null. Can transform to a new type U.

title: whenComplete — side effect on completion
description: Use whenComplete() to log the result (or error) of an async operation, without changing the outcome.
hints: It returns the same CompletableFuture<T> (does not change value)

solution.explanation: whenComplete() is for side effects (logging, metrics, cleanup) — it sees the result or exception but cannot change either. It returns a CompletableFuture<T> with the same value as the original (the BiConsumer's return is void). Compare: handle() can transform the value, whenComplete() cannot. If whenComplete's action throws, that exception is used instead of the original. Great for logging and auditing without affecting the data flow.

methodSignatures.method: CompletableFuture<T> whenComplete(BiConsumer<? super T, ? super Throwable> action)
methodSignatures.description: When this stage completes (success or failure), performs action. Returns CompletableFuture<T> with the same outcome.

title: completeExceptionally — manual failure injection
description: Create a CompletableFuture that is manually completed with an exception (e.g. for timeout or validation failure). Show how this propagates through the chain.

solution.explanation: completeExceptionally() manually fails a CompletableFuture, just as complete() manually succeeds it. This is useful for: custom timeout implementations, validation failures, or wrapping callbacks into CompletableFutures. Any stages chained after the future will see the exception and can handle it with exceptionally/handle. If the future was already completed, completeExceptionally() returns false and has no effect.

methodSignatures.description: Manually completes this future with an exception. Returns true if this invocation caused completion.
Manually completes this future with a value. Returns true if this invocation caused completion.
Runs a Runnable asynchronously (no return value). Returns CompletableFuture<Void>.

title: orTimeout and completeOnTimeout (Java 9+)
description: Use orTimeout() to fail a slow future after 300ms, and completeOnTimeout() to return a default value instead.

solution.explanation: orTimeout() (Java 9+) makes the future fail with TimeoutException if it hasn't completed within the given time. completeOnTimeout() (Java 9+) is the graceful alternative — it completes the future with a default value instead of an exception. Both use a ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor internally. Use orTimeout when you want to propagate the failure; use completeOnTimeout for graceful degradation.

methodSignatures.description: Java 9+. If not completed within timeout, completes exceptionally with TimeoutException.

methodSignatures.method: CompletableFuture<T> completeOnTimeout(T value, long timeout, TimeUnit unit)
methodSignatures.description: Java 9+. If not completed within timeout, completes normally with the given value.

title: thenRun — fire-and-forget after completion
description: After an order is placed asynchronously, use thenRun to trigger a post-completion action (e.g. send analytics event) that doesn't need the result.
hints: thenAccept gets the value; thenRun does not

solution.explanation: thenRun() executes a Runnable after the previous stage completes — it has no access to the result. This is ideal for fire-and-forget side effects like logging, metrics, or cleanup that don't need the computed value. Chaining thenAccept (which has the value) followed by thenRun (which doesn't) shows how each step narrows the type: String -> Void -> Void.

methodSignatures.description: When this stage completes, runs action with no access to the result. Returns CompletableFuture<Void>.

title: Real scenario: Order Checkout Pipeline
description: Build a complete async checkout pipeline: (1) validate cart, (2) fetch user and apply discount in parallel, (3) place order, (4) send confirmation email, (5) handle any failure gracefully.
hints: validateCart -> thenCompose to step 2+3 -> thenAccept -> exceptionally

solution.explanation: This pipeline shows all the key patterns together: (1) supplyAsync for independent async starts, (2) thenCompose for dependent steps, (3) thenCombine for parallel independent steps (fetchUser and applyDiscount run concurrently), (4) whenComplete for non-intrusive logging, (5) thenApply to transform the result, (6) exceptionally as the final safety net. The total time is roughly max(100 + max(200, 150)) = ~300ms instead of 550ms sequential.
